Phase 11 cut gate 3's (doc-lint) full-sweep cost ~7.9x (125,669ms -> 16,003ms) by removing a redundant duplicate invocation and parallelizing its per-extension loop across real child processes (CED_JOBS=4). Phase 12 decided on evidence to keep gate 8 serialized, closing COMPLETED WITH EXCLUSIONS after sharpening the original ambient-CPU-pressure rationale into a measured, currently-live memory-margin risk against a bounded ~14% maximum overlap upside. memory_candidates.content: When a script offers a strict/promotion mode (e.g. STRICT_X=1) whose ONLY observable difference from the default mode is that it ALSO performs an action the default mode already unconditionally logs/echoes (e.g. an advisory() that always prints 'ADVISORY: msg' and, only under strict mode, additionally calls fail() to print 'FAIL: msg' with the identical text), a caller invoking the script TWICE (once normal, once strict) purely to extract a derived count from the strict pass is very likely paying for a redundant full re-execution. Check whether the derived count (e.g. grep -c 'pattern' on strict output) can be reconstructed exactly from the single normal pass's own output plus a known transformation (here: baseline_matches + advisory_only_matches, since strict output = normal output + one extra FAIL line per ADVISORY line). Verify the reconstruction empirically against a live oracle (the real strict pass) on 0/1/2+ synthetic violations before removing the second invocation, not just by code-reading the logic.

To parallelize a sequential per-item loop whose item-processing functions mutate shared global state (counters, associative-array statuses, append-only line arrays) via well-known fixed-prefix output lines (e.g. 'FAIL: msg', 'ADVISORY: msg'), fork ONE REAL CHILD PROCESS per item (never a batched xargs -P shape -- measure both, one-process-per-unit often wins when the work is read-only and I/O/subprocess-spawn bound), capture each child's full stdout to its own file named with a zero-padded sequence number (preserving discovery order, not completion order), then after `wait`: (1) concatenate the per-item files IN SEQUENCE-NUMBER ORDER for byte-identical combined output, and (2) RE-DERIVE every piece of 'shared global state' by parsing the concatenated text for the same fixed-prefix markers the sequential version's own functions already emit unconditionally -- never by reading a child subshell's own (discarded) copy of the global back. This requires NO new IPC/locking mechanism: the markers already being printed to stdout ARE the IPC channel. Tune the worker cap empirically (don't assume higher is always better -- a cap of 4 can beat 8 on the same host from self-generated contention) and verify byte-identical output across several different worker counts, not just 'it doesn't crash'.

When deciding whether two independently-scheduled worker pools may safely run concurrently (e.g. an outer gate-level pool overlapping an inner suite-level pool each gate itself spawns), don't stop at core-count arithmetic (nproc vs. total requested workers) -- check actual live memory headroom (`free -h`: available, and swap used) on the real host, especially a shared, multi-session machine. A pool documented as an 'ambient CPU/core pressure precaution' may in practice be memory-bound instead (confirmed by directly measuring one pool's own peak RSS/peak `free -m` used during a real run and comparing it against the host's currently available memory) -- cores can be abundant (e.g. 24 cores, far above a 4-worker cap) while memory is the actual binding constraint. Size the maximum possible wall-clock benefit of overlapping (min(poolA_time, poolB_time)) before investing in cross-scheduler coordination machinery neither pool currently supports; a small bounded upside (e.g. ~14% of total) against a measured, currently-live resource-margin risk is often not worth the complexity and regression risk of building that coordination.
